newsitem.title: FRANCE: France heading for lower sugar crop - analysts.
newsitem.headline: France heading for lower sugar crop - analysts.

text.p: France should produce less sugar in 1996 than last year as results of the fourth sugar beet test by French producers showed the crop made only a partial recovery, industry analysts said on Monday.
"Results of the fourth and last test show the crop has improved but we are headed for a slight decline in sugar output this year," one analyst said.
Analysts said the national sugar yield may fall to between 9.4 and 9.6 tonnes per hectare from 9.8 tonnes last year.
Assuming the area would fall to 422,000 from 429,000 hectares, this would put the 1996 sugar output at between 3.9 and 4.05 million tonnes, down from 4.2 million tonnes last year.
Manufacturers' association SNFS said the test carried out on September 9 showed sugar weight per hectare fell by 5.7 percent to 9.382 tonnes from 9.951 tonnes in last year's fourth test.
This represented a 10.8 percent fall against the five-year average of 10.523 tonnes.
Analysts have blamed a prolonged dry spell during the growing period but had expected crop prospects to improve due to scattered rain in late August.
But unsufficient moisture levels between the third test carried out on August 26 and the fourth test limited the crop's progress, analysts said.
"Because there was not enough rain between August 26 and September 9, beet weight did not improve much. Sugar content however rose," one analyst said.
Root weight per hectare rose to 54.528 tonnes from 48.198 tonnes in the third test for 1996 but was still below 58.271 tonnes in the fourth test for 1995, SNFS statistics showed.

Sugar content rose to 17.21 percent from 15.87 percent in the third test and from 16.98 percent in the fourth test for 1995. The harvest traditionally starts in France in late September or early October.
